headline: Race rips fire as 67-degree water stacks bass on the flood — Plum Gut delivers
subhead: Current-swept edges holding slot fish to 37 inches as thermal gradient concentrates bait.
body_markdown:
The eastern Sound is finally cooking. Water temps hit 67 degrees this week and the bass responded exactly like they should — stacking up in the current breaks where the flood tide pushes bait against the structure. I've been working The Race and Plum Gut hard, and both spots are producing consistent action on the moving water.

Plum Gut has been the most reliable producer. The flood tide is the key — fish are sitting in the eddies on both sides of the main channel, ambushing bait as it gets swept through. I'm running 3-way rigs with 6-ounce sinkers to hold bottom in the 80-foot zone, tipping 1-ounce white bucktails with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets. The bass are hitting hard on the drop — no finesse required. Slot fish from 28 to 32 inches have been the bread and butter, with a few overs mixed in that go back.

The Race is more of a gamble but the payoff is bigger. When the current is screaming at 4 knots, the rip line forms a perfect feeding zone about 200 yards east of the main turbulence. I'm seeing bass to 37 inches working the edges where the clean water meets the white water. Same rig setup, but you need to be precise with your positioning — drift too far into the main rip and you'll lose gear, stay too far out and you're fishing dead water.

What's driving this bite is the thermal setup. The 67-degree water we're seeing is perfect bass temperature, and there's a solid gradient building between the Sound and the ocean water. Block Island is reading 62 degrees while we're holding 67 — that 5-degree difference is concentrating baitfish in our zone. The spearing are thick along the shoreline at Orient Point, and I'm seeing massive schools of sand eels getting pushed through the Gut on every tide change.

Timing is everything right now. The flood tide has been most productive, especially the first two hours when the current is building but not yet ripping. I'm getting to my spots 30 minutes before the tide turns and fishing through the peak flow. The ebb can produce, but you need to move shallower — the fish follow the bait into 40-50 feet on the back side of the tide.

Bluefish are also in the mix, especially at The Race. Big gator blues to 15 pounds are crashing the same bait schools as the bass. They're hitting bucktails hard and fighting like demons in the current. If you're targeting bass specifically, move away when the blues show up — they'll take over a spot fast.

Weather has been cooperating with light southwest winds, but that's changing. We've got a front approaching that will bring west winds to 15-20 knots by the weekend. That's actually good news for the fishing — west wind against the flood tide creates better structure and concentrates bait even tighter against the points.

The full moon is Friday, which means spring tides and maximum current flow. I'm planning to hit The Race on the big flood Friday night — when you get 5-knot current under a full moon, the bass go absolutely crazy. The key will be positioning just outside the main turbulence where you can still work a bucktail without getting destroyed.

Looking ahead, this 67-degree water should hold steady through the weekend. The thermal gradient between Sound and ocean water is only going to get stronger as we move into summer, which means the bait concentration should improve. I'm watching for the first real push of bunker schools — when those show up in size, the bass fishing will go from good to insane.
